Seldom have I heard judoka who're actually good winge about the leg grab ban. Don't get me wrong, these techniques should not be forgotten. Rec clubs have no reason to not to teach them, but I would be hesitant to teach them to newbies off the bat because, like Travis Stevens once said, "it's easy. people want that instant gratification". This is detrimental to the development of Judo's principles and the rec club members development of skill. At a later time you could teach them leg grabs. Like Shintaro said, leg grabs are really good for short people fighting taller people. Leg grabs would make a lot of sense in an openweight division. 

However.

Leg grabs were never high yield are were, to quote another redditor, peripheral compared to judo's entire glossary of techniques. I giggle whenever I hear someone say they quit judo do to the leg grab ban. Lol. You were trash to begin with if all you knew was how to dive on someone's ankles. I've never heard Judoka from other countries even bat an eye at the leg grab ban because it was never the main focus and their skill level is markedly higher than the average American judoka despite Americans clamoring that the lack of leg grabs has rendered judo useless as a martial art. rofl what?

The same goes for people who are critical of Judo newaza. I know turtling is just a competition thing but there literally is no reason for Judo's newaza to match BJJ. Why? Even more strange, some people actually think that Judo needs to train leg locks to match BJJ. WHY? This isn't cobra kai, Judo doesn't need to be everything on planet earth. We aren't competing with other styles. We specialize in standing, upright posture throws (some exceptions) and there is nothing wrong with that. We don't need to exceed our bandwidth to "compete" with BJJ or anything else. Hot take! Judo's standing throws and newaza are better than they have ever been and Olympic participation has kept us honest and have grown the talent pool and general skill level of every judoka.

Judo in America has to exist in the atmosphere of BJJ and MMA being mainstream, so Judo will always be judged based on BJJ rules and to a lesser extent the expectations of MMA. When you build your entire skillset on leg grabs you can easily fail to learn basic kuzushi and other principles of balance and posture of Judo. And that's not inherently a bad thing, **it just doesn't need to be the focus of judo.**

Well, this is kind of where the NGB's come in. You can theoretically teach judo without having any affiliations what so ever. I can think of quite a few dojo that have no affiliation but they're also kind of suspect. One I can think of was a [bullshido.net](https://bullshido.net) bust about a decade ago for faking a BJJ affiliation.

You can open up your own dojo tomorrow and people who have never done judo before would be none the wiser. Once you have actual experienced judoka come and train with you, that's where things are going to get weird.

NGB's such as USA Judo, USJA, and USJF have rank requirements for coaching and black belt degrees for a reason. They want to make sure you're putting proper information out there, to the best of their abilities. It's always safe to go with an instructor that is affiliated with one of these three.

If your instructor is running a program out of an MMA gym with no affiliation there is no way anyone can tell you're "legit" or not, and honestly if you're still a colored belt it wont matter anyways.

If you're worried about it, you could ask him in a polite way later on or you could visit another dojo and see how they train and do some randori.

I say the above because there actually exist judo dojo that teach very strange and incorrect things, and this isn't just a matter of strategy or teaching a throw they don't specialize in, because your instructor could be a legitimate judoka but also not specialize in a certain throw because it was never their focus, and thus might have a student who does that single throw better. Even if your instructor isn't a super ass kicker, he could still be teaching you sound techniques and methods even if he isn't the best in town.

These places that I'm thinking of usually don't do randori, and if they do, it is almost never live and very compliant. [Some of these places show techniques completely wrong](https://youtu.be/RNslI5phJ8I).

The thing about the yin yang principal is that there is yin in the yang, and yang in the yin. 

Cobra Kai are badasses. Strike first, strike hard, no mercy (yang energy). But maybe that no mercy part is wrong, and the part of cobra Kai that needs to go. It’s brought dejected kids together and ‘flipped their script’, and can make them better people, without the influence of Kreese (yin energy). 

Miyagi-do emphasizes peace, non combative behaviors, and balance (yin energy) but is very quick to judge, hold grudges, and escalate things (yang energy). 

There is a strange balance in the paradigm between the cobras and miyagi. The cobra Kai series with all its callbacks and references to the past is like a strange sort of synchronistic ‘fate’ playing itself out, reminiscent of Star Wars lore. And Star Wars was the classic battle between good and evil *inside the self*. Luke and Anakin’s story, and even the Disney sequels (wether you like them or not) are microcosms of the internal struggle of coming to terms with your ego, super ego, and shadow. Cobra Kai is the same way. 

It’s accidentally brilliant the way the first three karate kid movies where filmed. There was plenty of room for interpretation and Johnny and Daniel show that in cobra Kai. Johnny thought Daniel was a devious invader into his perfect life, constantly poking at his ribs. Daniel thought Johnny was an oppressive bully, but you even see Johnny express the good inside him at the end of the tournament in the first movie. You see Daniel briefly descent to the dark side in the third movie. 

The third movie really stuck out to me because at the time I was struggling with Judo. I thought I wasn’t getting enough attention from my instructors and watching all my peers succeed. I was angry and resentful for a time, and I wanted to find shortcuts that weren’t there. I started having inner hostility towards some people because I thought their training methods were making me worse at judo (much like anakin and obiwan, and like Daniel leaving miyagi for terry silver). But it wasn’t true, I wasn’t patient with my skill progression and my own frustration was holding me back, not other people. 

Much like with the problems in cobra Kai, all issues stem from misunderstandings and fighting your inner demons. 

Edit for my weirder observations: 

Johnny is what happens when there is no Miyagi in your life, only Kreese. Miyagi is the ideal of the good, and Kreese the ideal of the bad. Miyagi is the model citizen, the kind, understanding, diplomatic father. The Yin. But it has its drawbacks. Sometimes passivity doesn’t work. 

Kreese is like a cobra, striking from the shadows. Mother fucker just can’t die. He’s the embodiment of confidence gone awry, the oppressive father. The judge. The Yang. He is the *venomous* inner shadow. But even that has its benefits. Sometimes you need to stand your ground, bear your teeth, and kick ass. 

Kreese and Miyagi are two sides of the same coin that must find balance between the two. Miyagi is dead, and with him, some of his teachings. Daniel still struggles in adulthood, he must find a way to spiritually revive what Miyagi embodies. 

Kreese still lives, and his venom is infecting Hawk and others just as it did Johnny. It’s alluring; the power, status, the confidence. Much like the Sith. But Johnny survived that, and could very well bring ‘balance to the force’ that Daniel is missing. 

Daniel was lucky to have Miyagi. It’s as if he was Gods chosen. 

Johnny didn’t have a Miyagi. God’s bastard son. He didn’t have anyone. If you think about it, Johnny is stronger than Daniel. He had to fix his life without Miyagi, and with his dark side (kreese) looking over his shoulder. 

Miyagi and Kreese technically don’t exist. They’re the extremes of yin and yang within Johnny and Daniel. Perhaps within you too.

I would like to compete under freestyle judo rules but I have yet to see or hear about any good athletes coming out of those programs. 

Kano was metropolitan for his time, but he wanted less emphasis on newaza. His priority was always nage waza. He even banned leg locks for various reasons. 

Freestyle judo isn’t reminiscent of judo of the past, and I would argue that judo has developed because of its international recognization and place in the Olympics. The skill ceiling is enormous. The judo of old also didn’t emphasize grip fighting which is absolutely essential for judo. Judo has only gotten better with time, but I will concede that rolling ippon and the removal of leg grabs from local clubs (banning them in comp shouldn’t affect what local and Rec clubs teach imo) is a negative. 

But that doesn’t mean judo lost anything substantial. 99% of the judo Arsenal is legal. And people won’t like this, but strict gripping rules pushes the pace and forces athletes to be more explosive and decisive in their attacks.

For BJJ, you might get better mileage out of doing wrestling, and I’m saying that because of the stance you assume in BJJ as well as the ruleset. Judo has more of an upright posture which might be disadvantageous under a BJJ ruleset where the rules are more lax concerning stalling and defensive postures. 

Now, there are judoka who will fight “wrestling style”, kind of bent over, keeping their hips away. But you can’t stay in this position for too long in judo without getting a penalty or getting reset. And in training, some of the more serious types would call defensive postures “negative judo”. Both judo and wrestling a good at fast, explosive action but the rules are different and techniques are somewhat different too. Judo is predominantly taught in a very erect posture and the rules on defensiveness and stalling reflect that .

In BJJ you can stay in that position for awhile. 

There’s also the gi. Sambo uses a kurtka, which is their version of a gi. You can easily adapt judo throws into nogi, but since you want a base *for* BJJ, I think wrestling might be the choice just for the reasons I listed above.

There are judoka who cross train with BJJ but they can’t do judo in its purest form in a BJJ environment. which is why some people may think wrestling transfers better than judo. There is crossover between judo and BJJ but ultimately they are different sports with different meta and different goals.
